content:
(copy and paste from Opus 5.5; collaboratively-executed)

On average we're about 5.5x slower than native Roc. That's the geometric mean of the five work benchmarks

the reveal: I have a LuaJIT backend, lowered from LIR, working for Roc, that passes the entire test suite except for 1 failure that the native Roc also currently fails on; it is far faster than Python, Ruby, etc. as a "scripting language" not requiring compilation, while letting you enjoy all of the Roc niceties. :grinning:

I also have a few bugfixes for Roc proper to PR, just need to get my github signing ability back (long story)

Why this heresy: I liked LuaJIT (speed, simplicity) but not better than Roc; I also already have luajit installed everywhere, and wanted access to Roc without (yet) installing the whole chain everywhere.

Thoughts?
This reminds me of a segment from Richard Feldman's podcast Software Unscripted where he and Louis Pilfold discuss how Gleam came to having Javascript as a compile target.
I'm not knowledgeable on how much it affected the core mission of Gleam. So, I wonder how much a LuaJIT backend would affect Roc?

as a "scripting language" not requiring compilation, while letting you enjoy all of the Roc niceties.

AFAIK, the goal for Roc is to have sub-second compilation time for debug builds. Basically usable as a scripting language, even in AOT mode.

I like that! And I already built some tooling that basically caches a compiled version of an executable script (while allowing you to continue to run the script directly, but it does an "exec" underneath)

Ah, forgot to mention that it has some rudimentary interop as well (running luajit code from the roc side and receiving typed values back, running roc code from the luajit side with the same types of side-effects)

Since LuaJIT is trivially-embeddable everywhere, this also now means Roc is trivially-embeddable everywhere
I'd like to know if WASM (which is quite fast) might end up the interoperation lingua-franca at the lowest layers
What is the advantage of this over a native binary?
It's deployable everywhere, and you wouldn't even need LuaJIT installed.
I routinely use 3 OS'es on any given day. ;)
And 2 chip archs. ;)
I have a NixOS machine for pure dev, a Mac for secondary dev and "life apps", and a Windows box for gaming, testing my Windows ports and NixOS-on-WSL

About a year ago I decided to just stick LuaJIT everywhere and replace any Bash scripting that was more than 15 lines or so with Lua. Everything instantly became more maintainable, more portable and much faster.

I'd love a portable Roc solution that didn't require me to rebuild it everywhere. But also, Luajit really is kind of everywhere. Finance software to games. Cheap embed with C FFI. Roc being able to ride on that without much reconfiguration might be a foot in the door where it might not otherwise be.
(At the cost of being 5-10x slower. But logically correct.)
This would add lot of complexity to the Roc compiler, at the benefit of removing a few lines of shell code for deployment.
Roc can cross-compile from any host to any other arch and OS combination. This means that you can build your scripts on one machine for all of your devices.
How do you deploy your scripts?

It already works. There's no added complexity. It's lowered from LIR, which is generated by the compiler, and spits out a .roc.lua if you just specify the build option. But I need to play with it more. Maybe there's a complexity I'm missing.

I sync scripts through git, usually with Nix controlling deps.
And truth be told, it's not legit unless it's battle-tested in prod, and this hasn't been.
How is LuaJIT better than WASI? Is it lighter?

It's lowered from LIR, which is generated by the compiler, and spits out a .roc.lua if you just specify the build option.

So it's a separate tool, with no modifications required to the Roc compiler?

How is LuaJIT better than WASI

Good question. Well for one thing it's battle-tested and already installed in way more places, many of which would surprise you (it did me). LuaJIT has trivial C FFI access, for one thing. It's also more legible to humans than WASI (if you deal with it via WAT). And honestly, part of me was thinking "what's the best first language to teach my son?" and both Roc and Lua were at the top of that list for fairly different, but both legitimate, reasons. ;) ("Learning a language" may be a thing of the past, soon?) But honestly, yeah, WASM is coming in hot here, and I honestly think it's going to sort of be the next LLVM in terms of "popular intermediate build target."

AI writes LuaJIT well, but (funny thing) it argued against me having it write Lua and actually said Roc was better, especially when considering agent/human collab (this is the current belief over here, btw, about where things are going). Of course, it said this after the project was already working. LOL.

It cited Roc's immaturity as a strong argument against it, though. (But that's just time and effort to surmount.)

It's mostly an experiment. Giving Roc access to LuaJIT code also gives it the same trivial C FFI access Luajit has, which might make it easier to integrate with some things.

"Learning a language" may be a thing of the past, soon?

Definitely not. It's fun. Probably even more new languages will be created, with LLM help in the compiler development.

Agreed. It is always going to be fun to some. Which is good, because there's a distinct possibility that no matter how smart AI gets, it may simply create more-difficult-to-run-down bugs, and then we need the programmer-humans again!
And also agree on even more languages... and language forks. The cost of code creativity (CCC?) has gone way down.
This being a perfect example. This experiment took about a day (as in, Opus 5.5 with my oversight literally took about 24 hours to complete it.)

I know a guy who was able to use Clojure in a Java shop (salesforce, sigh) only because Clojure was a JVM language.

If someone somewhere had already accepted Lua into their setup, now someone can perhaps shoehorn Roc in. ;)

(nonsequitur)
Another thing that might be fun to do is putting a Roc backplane on my Aedicule sideproject
https://github.com/pmarreck/aedicule
The idea behind Aedicule is "universal GUI frontplane" providing drawing/sound/sprite/input primitives, and controls via gpui_component. It's built in Rust and uses GPUI from the Zeditor project. The backplane can be built in anything. Currently it only supports WAT (webassembly/webassembly text) but it's pluggable. I could probably easily add Roc, assuming its wasm output works, and then you'd get the same code running identically as a performant GUI in an app across 3 OS'es as well as web browsers (which is what the handful of existing demos at https://pmarreck.github.io/aedicule/ all already accomplish).
